content: The tibia, commonly referred to as the shin bone, is the larger of the two bones located in the lower leg beneath the knee in vertebrates. In human anatomy, the tibia is positioned medially (towards the midline of the body) and anteriorly (towards the front) relative to the fibula, the other bone in the lower leg. It is the second-longest bone in the human body, surpassed only by the femur. The tibia articulates superiorly with the femur and patella, laterally with the fibula, and inferiorly with the bones of the ankle. In males, the tibia is oriented vertically and runs parallel to the tibia on the opposite side. In females, however, the tibia has a slightly oblique downward and lateral direction to accommodate the greater obliquity of the femur. Structurally, the tibia has a prismoid shape. It is expanded at its upper end, where it contributes to the knee joint, narrows in its lower third, and then slightly enlarges again at its distal end, though to a lesser extent. The tibia is connected to the fibula by an interosseous membrane, forming a type of joint known as a syndesmosis. The arterial blood supply to the tibia is derived from two main sources: the nutrient artery, which serves as the primary source, and periosteal vessels, which originate from the anterior tibial artery. The right knee joint, shown from various perspectives, including posterior, anterior (highlighting interior ligaments), and sagittal sections. The capsule of the right knee joint, displayed in both distended lateral and posterior aspects. The capsule of the left talocrural articulation, shown in a distended lateral view. Coronal sections through the right talocrural and talocalcaneal joints. Oblique sections of the left intertarsal and tarsometatarsal articulations, illustrating the synovial cavities. Cross-sections through the middle of the leg.
